creative.body:
If you're on Ozempic, Wegovy, or Mounjaro and your stomach feels like it's full of cement, you can't stop burping sulfur, and you haven't had a normal bowel movement in weeks, I need you to hear this.

Because what I'm about to tell you is going to make you furious.

Here's what's happening right now:

One — the medication that's finally silencing your food noise is quietly wrecking your digestion from the top down. Not just "causing constipation." Something deeper.

Two — when you bring it up to your doctor, they're going to tell you to take Miralax and drink more water.

And three — there's a reason that advice doesn't work. And a reason nobody's telling you why.

I know this because I've watched it happen from the other side of the exam room.

I've been a nurse for 23 years. GI clinic. I've seen things that would make you lose sleep. I've held the hand of a woman who was vomiting bile after a bowel obstruction. I've watched a 74-year-old man cry because he couldn't pass a stool for sixteen days and thought he was dying. I've been in that room for thousands of patients with every digestive problem you can imagine.

But the thing I can't stop thinking about is a 58-year-old woman named Karen who sat on the exam table in our clinic and cried because she hadn't had a bowel movement in eleven days.

Let me tell you what happened to her. Not the clinical version. The real one.

She'd been on Wegovy for five months. Down 31 pounds. Bloodwork was beautiful. A1C improved. Blood pressure down. On paper she was a textbook success story. The kind of patient you put in a presentation.

I took her vitals and asked the standard questions. She answered everything fine until I asked, "Any digestive issues?"

And she just stopped. Looked at the floor. Then looked at me with this expression I've seen a thousand times — the one where someone is deciding whether to tell the truth or say what they think the doctor wants to hear.

"I haven't gone to the bathroom in eleven days," she said.

I put down my clipboard.

She started talking fast, the way people do when they've been holding something in for months and someone finally asks. The bloating so severe she looked six months pregnant by the end of every day. She couldn't button her pants by noon. She'd stopped wearing anything with a waistband and lived in stretchy leggings, which defeated the purpose of losing 31 pounds in the first place.

The sulfur burps. Hot, rotten, like eggs that had been sitting in the sun. So unpredictable she'd stopped going out to eat. She told me about her grandson's baseball game the month before. She was sitting in the bleachers cheering and a burp came up so bad her grandson turned around and said "Grandma, what's that smell?" loud enough for every parent in a ten-foot radius to hear. She pretended to look confused. She told him she didn't smell anything. She left at the fourth inning and cried in the parking lot.

She told me about the road trip. Driving to her daughter's house four hours away. By hour two the pressure was so bad she was doubled over in the passenger seat. Her husband pulled off at a rest stop. She locked herself in a gas station bathroom and gave herself an enema from a kit she'd started carrying in her purse. In a gas station bathroom on the side of I-40 because the pain was a ten out of ten and she couldn't make it another two hours.

She told me about her medicine cabinet. She'd been through all of it. Miralax every single day for three months. Dulcolax when the Miralax didn't work. Colace twice a day. Mag citrate. Fiber gummies. Smooth Move tea. Senna. Prune juice she hid behind the orange juice because she was embarrassed. She had a spreadsheet on her phone tracking the last time she'd gone.

And then she said the thing I hear from every single one of these women:

"But I've lost 31 pounds. So I just deal with it."

The medication is giving her the body she's wanted for thirty years. But she's too sick to enjoy living in it.

Sound familiar?

The doctor spent nine minutes with her. I know because I checked.

He told Karen that constipation was a very common side effect. Asked if she was drinking enough water. Suggested increasing her fiber. Maybe trying Miralax.

Karen looked at him and said, "I've been taking Miralax every day for three months."

He paused. Typed something into the chart. Said they could try Linzess. Or consider lowering her dose.

Karen's face went white. "Lower my dose? I've lost thirty-one pounds."

He nodded sympathetically. Said follow up in six weeks.

She left. I walked her out. At the door she turned and said, "He didn't hear a single thing I said, did he?"

I wanted to tell her the truth. Instead I said, "Give the Linzess a try and call us if it doesn't help."

She didn't call back. They never do. Because the weight is still coming off and they've decided the suffering is the price of admission. They've made their peace with the spreadsheet and the gas station enema and the parking lot cry and the mints in every pocket and the bleacher section incident they'll never forget.

But Karen broke something in me.

Not because she was the first. She wasn't even close. She was the fifty-eighth. I'd been keeping count since the GLP-1 wave started. Fifty-eight women in fourteen months who sat in that exam room with some version of the same story. The same side effects. The same medicine cabinet. The same advice from the same doctors. The same resignation in their voice when they said "But I've lost X pounds."

Karen was just the one who made me stop. Because when I said "Give the Linzess a try," I heard myself, and I realized I'd been saying some version of that sentence for fourteen months without once asking a question that should have been obvious.

Why doesn't any of this work?

Not why doesn't Miralax work sometimes. Why doesn't ANY of it work? Why is every single one of these women trying everything on the shelf and none of it making a real difference?

So I went down a rabbit hole. Not patient forums. Not Facebook groups. Not the same recycled advice every health website copies from each other. The actual studies. PubMed. Gastroenterology journals. Motility research.

And what I found at 1 AM on my night off, sitting at my kitchen table with cold coffee and twenty-three browser tabs open, made me want to walk back into that exam room and apologize to every woman I'd ever handed a Miralax recommendation to.

Because we were all treating the wrong organ.

Think of digestion as a highway. Food enters at the on-ramp — the stomach. Travels through the middle — the small intestine. Exits at the off-ramp — the colon.

When you hear "constipation," you think colon. Everyone does. The doctors do. The products do. That's where things exit. That's where the blockage must be.

But GLP-1 medications don't work at the off-ramp. They slow things down at the on-ramp. That's literally the mechanism. That's why they work for weight loss. Your stomach loses its rhythm. Food sits there for hours — sometimes days. It ferments. That's where the sulfur gas comes from. It dries out and hardens. That's the cement feeling.

By the time anything reaches the colon — if it reaches the colon — it's already a brick. The colon isn't blocked. It's practically empty. The problem was never at the exit.

And every single product in Karen's medicine cabinet was aimed at the exit.

Miralax pulls water into the colon to soften what's sitting there. But nothing was sitting there. The blockage was in her stomach, six feet upstream.

Fiber gummies add bulk to help things pass through the colon. When food can't get out of the stomach, adding bulk is packing more cars onto a highway where the on-ramp is closed.

Dulcolax forces the colon to contract. But you can squeeze an empty tube all day. Nothing comes out if nothing went in.

Smooth Move tea stimulates the lower intestine. Same problem. You can't flush a pipe from the bottom when the clog is at the top.

Linzess — the prescription the doctor offered as his escalation — works by increasing fluid secretion in the intestine. Still downstream. Still six feet below the problem. Different mechanism, same wrong address.

Karen spent months and hundreds of dollars treating an off-ramp that wasn't even clogged. And I spent fourteen months handing her — and fifty-seven women before her — directions to the same wrong exit.

That's the part that kept me up at night.

So the question became: what actually works on the stomach?

I spent three nights reading. Followed citations from paper to paper. Pulled up full-text studies from journals I hadn't opened since nursing school. Three things kept surfacing across different research tracks, and each one addressed a different piece of the problem.

First — a compound called apigenin. Found in high concentrations in celery. It supports the vagus nerve — the nerve that controls stomach contractions, the nerve that tells the stomach when to push food through. GLP-1 medications essentially mute that signal. Apigenin was showing up in motility studies as a way to gently support it again. Not override the medication. Not force anything. Like turning the volume back up on a speaker someone turned down.

That was the first piece. Wake the stomach up.

But even with the stomach moving, there's a backlog. Weeks of slow digestion mean bacteria have been producing hydrogen sulfide — sulfur gas — faster than the body can clear it. The burps. The rotten egg taste. The bleacher incident. Getting things moving again doesn't fix the gas that's already forming.

The second piece was chlorophyllin — a concentrated form of chlorophyll. It binds directly to hydrogen sulfide and neutralizes it before it rises as gas. Doesn't mask the smell. Doesn't cover it up. Disarms the molecule that creates it.

Two pieces. But I kept reading. Because even with the stomach moving and the gas handled, everything downstream was still backed up. Weeks of stalled motility mean the small intestine and colon are congested even once the stomach starts working again.

The third piece was a specific type of soluble prebiotic fiber. Not the bulk fiber every doctor recommends — that's the last thing a backed-up system needs. Insoluble fiber on top of a jammed system is like adding bricks to a traffic jam. This was low-bulk, gel-forming. Draws moisture in. Softens what's stuck without adding volume. Lets things clear once the stomach starts working again.

Three things. Wake up the stomach. Neutralize the sulfur. Soften the downstream backup without making it worse.

Motility. Gas neutralization. Downstream flow. All three working together.

That's when I understood why Karen's medicine cabinet never stood a chance. Every product addressed one piece — and most of them addressed the wrong piece entirely.

I started looking for something that combined all three. Found motility supplements with ginger extract but nothing for the gas. Found chlorophyll drops with no motility support. Found fiber blends that would have made everything worse — insoluble bulk on top of an already jammed system. Plenty of products with one piece. A couple with two. Nothing with all three in the right forms.

Then I found a small company I'd never heard of in a forum thread buried about thirty comments deep. They'd built a gummy specifically for people on GLP-1 medications. Not a general digestive supplement repackaged with a new label. Not a probiotic claiming to fix everything. Something designed from the ground up for this exact problem.

Motilli.

Celery juice concentrate standardized for apigenin. Chlorophyllin. Low-bulk soluble prebiotic fiber.

I'll be honest. My first reaction was skepticism. I've been a nurse for 23 years. I've watched patients waste thousands on supplements that do nothing. I've seen the labels that promise everything and the bottles that deliver nothing. And "celery juice gummies" is not the kind of phrase that makes a medical professional sit up and pay attention.

But I checked each ingredient against the studies I'd been reading for three nights. Apigenin — present, at a real concentration, from actual celery juice extract, not a token sprinkle. Chlorophyllin — present, not just decorative chlorophyll for color. Soluble prebiotic fiber — the right kind, low-bulk, gel-forming.

Motility support. Gas neutralization. Downstream flow. All three. In one gummy. At concentrations that matched the research I'd been reading.

The company was small. No massive marketing budget. No celebrity endorsements. Just the formulation, a clean label, and a 90-day money-back guarantee — which told me something, because companies that are guessing don't offer to let your gut decide for three months.

I ordered two bottles that night. One for me to evaluate. One for Karen.

I should tell you — I'm 46. I'm not on a GLP-1. But I've had sluggish digestion for years, the kind you develop after two decades of night shifts, hospital food, and stress eating at 3 AM. I started taking two gummies every morning alongside my coffee.

By day four I noticed my digestion felt different. Smoother. Less of the heavy brick-in-the-stomach feeling I'd lived with so long I'd stopped noticing it. By week two I realized I hadn't taken a Tums in ten days — something I used to do nightly. That wasn't the target audience. That wasn't the intended use. But it told me the motility piece was doing something real. That mattered to me professionally before I put my name behind it with a patient.

I called Karen the next week. She'd stopped coming to our clinic. I wasn't surprised. I told her I'd found something I wanted her to try. Didn't oversell it. Just said it worked on the stomach instead of the colon, and I thought it was worth thirty days.

She was quiet for a long time. Then she said, "At this point I'll try anything."

Two gummies a day. She started the following Monday.

Day three she texted: "Nothing yet."

I told her to give it time. This wasn't a laxative. It wasn't forcing anything. It was supporting the stomach's ability to move food through the way it's supposed to.

Day five: "Bloating feels a little less. Maybe placebo."

Day ten: "I went this morning. On my own. No Miralax. No enema. Just went."

That text shouldn't have hit as hard as it did. But it did. Because I knew about the eleven days. The gas station. The spreadsheet. The enema kit in her purse.

Week two — the sulfur burps were fading. Not gone. But the hot, rotten, unpredictable eruptions that made her leave her grandson's game at the fourth inning were becoming smaller. Quieter. Less frequent.

Week three — she told me they were gone. She'd eaten pasta the night before and waited for it. Waited for the sulfur to build. It never came.

Month one — she stopped by the clinic. Not as a patient. To see me. She'd thrown out the spreadsheet. Still on Wegovy. Still losing weight. Still had the silence where food didn't run her brain every waking hour.

But she wasn't paying the tax anymore.

She'd also done something I didn't expect. She'd added up what she'd been spending on the products that weren't working. Miralax, Dulcolax, Colace, mag citrate, fiber gummies, Smooth Move, senna, prune juice. She showed me the number on her phone. Over four months, she'd spent more on OTC products that targeted the wrong organ than she would have spent on a year of something that actually worked on the right one.

Month two — her husband noticed. She was going out again. Saying yes to dinners. Staying for the whole visit at the grandkids' house instead of disappearing every thirty minutes.

"He said I seem like myself again," she told me. "He didn't know I'd been gone."

Month three — I ran into her at a grocery store. She was buying food. Real food. Not the safe list she'd been living on for months because she was terrified of what anything heavy would do to her stomach. She had chicken and pasta and vegetables in her cart. She smiled at me and said, "I ate dinner last night and didn't think about it once."

She went to her grandson's next game. Stayed the whole time. Nobody smelled anything. Because there was nothing to smell.

Since Karen, I've quietly shared the same research with eleven other women. On my own time. Not in the exam room. Over coffee. Over text. In parking lots after clinic hours. Every one of them had some version of the same story — months of OTC products that never worked, doctors who said drink more water, a medicine cabinet that looked like a pharmacy aisle, and the same quiet resignation that this was just the cost of losing weight.

Every one of them showed improvement within two to three weeks once something was finally working on the stomach instead of the colon. Not all at the same speed. Not all with the same symptoms resolving first. But the pattern was consistent. Bloating first. Then the sulfur. Then bowel regularity. Because that's the order the highway clears — on-ramp first, then middle, then off-ramp.

One woman — a 62-year-old retired teacher on Mounjaro — texted me after three weeks and said, "I ate Thanksgiving dinner with my family for the first time in two years without spending the rest of the night on the bathroom floor."

That's not a clinical outcome. That's a life.

Here's what I need you to hear. From a nurse who spent 23 years inside the system and 14 months watching it fail the same women over and over:

Your doctors aren't lying when they say constipation is a common side effect. They're right. But they're wrong about where it starts. And because they're wrong about where it starts, every solution they offer is aimed at the wrong place.

Motility. Gas neutralization. Downstream flow. That's not a mystery. That's mechanics. And until something addresses all three, you can take every laxative in the pharmacy and still end up on day eleven with a spreadsheet and an enema kit in your purse.

You don't have to choose between the weight loss and your digestion. That's not the deal. Nobody told you that was the deal when they handed you the prescription. You don't owe your gut as payment for your waistline.

And you don't have to keep spending money on products that work six feet below the problem.

I left a link below. Order one bottle. Take two gummies a day for 30 days. If nothing changes, send it back. They'll refund every penny. No questions. No hassle. Ninety days to decide.

But pay attention to the first week. Watch the bloating. Watch the sulfur. Keep your own notes. And when the spreadsheet starts looking different — when the numbers start shrinking from days to hours — you'll know the same thing I knew sitting at my kitchen table at 1 AM with twenty-three browser tabs open.

We were treating the wrong organ. And we don't have to anymore.

Karen didn't.

And she's back at the baseball games.
creative.title: Every laxative I tried was aimed at the wrong end of my body
